Design your workload to adapt to changes in demand
Demand on a workload rarely holds steady. Traffic grows over months,
    spikes during a sales event, and falls away overnight, and a
    component can degrade at any point along the way. Provisioning a
    fixed amount of capacity to cover the highest expected peak wastes
    money during quiet periods and still runs short when a peak exceeds
    the estimate. An elastic workload adds and removes resources
    automatically so that capacity tracks demand, but that elasticity
    only holds up when the scaling is automated, the signals reflect
    real load, and the limits have been proven under test.
This capability covers how an organization designs a workload to
    match resources to demand: provisioning and scaling through
    automation rather than manually, recovering capacity when a
    component becomes impaired, adding resources as healthy demand
    grows, and validating the whole arrangement with load tests that
    find the breaking point before customers do.
REL07: How do you design your workload to adapt to changes
            in demand?
REL07-BP01 Use automation when obtaining or scaling resources
REL07-BP02 Obtain resources upon detection of impairment to a workload
REL07-BP03 Obtain resources upon detection that more resources are needed for a workload
REL07-BP04 Load test your workload
Capability intent
Infrastructure is defined as code and provisioned through
          automated pipelines, so every environment is built the same
          way and every change is reviewable.
Resources scale out and scale in automatically within defined
          limits, so capacity follows demand instead of a static
          estimate.
Impairment is detected from health signals and answered with a
          defined response that restores capacity, rather than waiting
          on a customer report.
Demand-driven scaling uses a metric that tracks load in both
          directions, with headroom for a burst to be served while
          replacements come online.
Scaling policies and capacity plans are proven through load
          testing against a production-scale environment, and re-tested
          as demand grows.
Common issues to watch for
Resources are provisioned manually through the console, so
          environments drift apart and a rebuild produces a subtly
          different system that fails in production.
A scaling metric is chosen that does not track demand in both
          directions, such as memory utilization, so the workload scales
          out under load and never scales back in.
Scaling targets are set close to full utilization, so existing
          capacity is exhausted before latent scaling brings
          replacements to full service.
Health checks confirm only that a process is listening, not
          that it can serve requests, so an impaired component is
          reported as healthy.
Load testing runs against an environment that does not match
          production, or stops just above expected load, so the real
          breaking point is never found.
Load testing happens once at launch and is never repeated, so
          a limit that sat above traffic at launch moves into range
          unnoticed as demand climbs.
